title: the day the whole people says sorry together
hookLine: the day the whole people says sorry together

cards: It's the tenth day of the seventh month, just after sunset, and the synagogue is full, with faces that don't come every week. Some are dressed in white. Some are wearing sneakers under their good clothes.
The fast began before sunset, and it won't end until the stars come out tomorrow night.
Then a cantor begins a melody so old and so familiar that some people cry before a word is sung, and it's sung three times, each time a little louder.
From this evening to the next, a whole people will say sorry, together. Today: Yom Kippur.

teach.b: Yom Kippur means the day of atonement. The Torah sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the autumn, and tells the people to afflict their souls, which the rabbis understood as a fast.
So from evening to evening: no food, no water, no leather shoes, no washing for pleasure.
Children don't fast, and neither does anyone whose health it would put at risk: Jewish law says protecting life comes first, so eating then is the right thing to do.
White clothes are common, like angels, some say, who don't need to eat. The evening begins with Kol Nidre, the melody from the start, whose Aramaic words release vows. And then the confessions.

Not I have sinned. We have. One confession runs through the Hebrew alphabet, a wrong for every letter, and everyone says every line, lightly tapping their chest, including lines about things they personally never did.
The whole community stands together as one. Nobody is singled out, and nobody gets to pretend they're above it. But the day has a limit, and the rabbis wrote it down plainly.
Yom Kippur atones for what's between a person and God. For what's between you and another person, it doesn't, until you've made it right with them.
So in the days before, the custom is to call, write, knock on doors, and ask forgiveness.

teach.h: THE FAST DOESN'T REPLACE THE CALL.
teach.b: The fast doesn't replace the phone call. In the afternoon, the story of Jonah is read: a whole city that turns around and is given another chance.

teach.h: NEILAH — THE CLOSING OF THE GATES.
teach.b: As the sun goes down, the last service is called Neilah, the closing of the gates.

teach.h: ONE LONG BLAST OF THE SHOFAR.
teach.b: The doors of the ark stay open, the room stands, and at nightfall one long blast of the ram's horn ends it. Then everybody goes home and eats.

how: On Yom Kippur Jews fast from sunset to nightfall the next day, wear no leather shoes, often dress in white, and spend much of the day in synagogue, from Kol Nidre in the evening to Neilah and the final shofar blast at nightfall; in the days before, it's customary to ask forgiveness of people one has wronged.

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: the evening melody, sung three times
make it right with them first

s: on Yom Kippur each person confesses only their own wrongs
the confessions are in the plural: we have sinned. everyone says every line.
Yom Kippur alone doesn't fix wrongs between people
for those, you have to make it right with the person first.
Yom Kippur is a day of feasting
it's a fast, from sunset to nightfall the next day.

games.q: you hurt a friend this year. Yom Kippur is next week. what did the rabbis say to do?
o: fast on Yom Kippur. that covers it.
go to your friend and make it right first.
games.why: Yom Kippur atones between a person and God; between people, only once you've made peace with them.

practice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one person you owe an apology, big or small, recent or old. Don't write the speech yet.
Just picture their face, and picture the moment of saying it. Notice what makes it hard. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to make the call.

wordCard.voice: Yom Kippur. The day of atonement: a day of fasting, confessing together, and closing gates. Eighteenth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the day of atonement. the Torah calls it yom ha-kippurim.

carryVoice: Your line: you can start over. A whole people says so, out loud, every year. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Yoma 8:5–6 (the sick are fed on Yom Kippur; danger to life overrides the fast)
Leviticus 16:29–31; 23:27–32 (the tenth day of the seventh month; afflict your souls)
Mishnah Yoma 8:1 (the five afflictions) and 8:9 (between person and person)
The Yom Kippur liturgy: Kol Nidre, the alphabetical confession (Ashamnu), Neilah
The book of Jonah (read on Yom Kippur afternoon)
